questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: A.5 Galilean and special relativity (AHL): time dilation, proper time, length contraction
questions.topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
questions.challenge_mechanism: The unknown is the speed, and it appears inside the Lorentz factor, so the equation is implicit: students must solve for gamma algebraically rather than substitute into a formula, then reconcile two frames that disagree about both distance and time.
questions.question:
A spacecraft travels in a straight line from Earth to a star. In the Earth frame the star is $8.0$ light years away. The spacecraft travels at constant speed $v$ and the astronauts measure the journey as taking $3.0$ years.

A light year is the distance travelled by light in one year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the Lorentz factor $\gamma$ and hence the speed $v$, as a fraction of $c$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the distance between Earth and the star as measured in the spacecraft frame.

parts.label: c
parts.text: On arrival the astronauts send a radio message to Earth. Calculate the time interval, measured on Earth, between the launch of the spacecraft and the receipt of the message.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain, without contradiction, how the astronauts can cover $8.0$ light years in $3.0$ years of their own time.

questions.answer:
Work in units of years and light years, so that $c=1\ \mathrm{ly\,yr^{-1}}$ and $v=\beta c$ with $\beta=v/c$.

**(a)**  Earth-frame journey time: $t=\dfrac{8.0}{\beta}$ years.  **(A1)**

The astronauts measure the **proper** time (both events — departure and arrival — occur at the same place in the spacecraft), so

$$\tau=\frac{t}{\gamma}=\frac{8.0}{\beta}\sqrt{1-\beta^{2}}=3.0$$  **(M1)(A1)**

Squaring:  $\dfrac{64(1-\beta^{2})}{\beta^{2}}=9 \Rightarrow 64-64\beta^{2}=9\beta^{2} \Rightarrow \beta^{2}=\dfrac{64}{73}$  **(M1)**

$$\beta=\frac{8}{\sqrt{73}}=0.9363,\qquad \gamma=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\frac{64}{73}}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{9/73}}=\frac{\sqrt{73}}{3}=2.85$$  **(A1)(A1)**

$$v=0.936c\ \ (\approx2.81\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}).$$

Limiting-case check: for a subluminal speed the Lorentz factor must be real and greater than $1$. Since $\beta^{2}=64/73<1$, the speed satisfies $v<c$, and $\gamma=\sqrt{73}/3=2.85>1$; both conditions hold, so the algebra is self-consistent.  **(R1)**

**(b)**  The Earth–star distance is the **proper** length (the two endpoints are at rest in the Earth frame), so it is contracted in the spacecraft frame:

$$L=\frac{L_{0}}{\gamma}=\frac{8.0}{2.848}=2.81\ \mathrm{ly}$$  **(M1)(A1)(A1)**

**(c)**  Earth-frame journey time:  $t=\dfrac{8.0}{0.9363}=8.54\ \mathrm{yr}$.  **(A1)**

The message travels $8.0$ ly at speed $c$, taking a further $8.0$ yr.  **(A1)**

$$\text{Total}=8.54+8.0=16.5\ \mathrm{yr}$$  **(A1)**

**(d)**  In the spacecraft frame the distance to be covered is not $8.0$ ly but the contracted distance $2.81$ ly from (b).  **(A1)**  The star approaches at $0.936c$, so the journey takes

$$\frac{2.81\ \mathrm{ly}}{0.936\ \mathrm{ly\,yr^{-1}}}=3.0\ \mathrm{yr},$$

which is exactly the astronauts' measured time.  **(A1)**

There is no contradiction: distance and time intervals are frame-dependent, but the **relative** speed between spacecraft and star is $0.936c$ in *both* frames, so nothing exceeds $c$. The Earth observer says the trip took $8.54$ yr of Earth time; the astronauts say it took $3.0$ yr of their own time and that the distance was shorter. Both are correct.  **(A1)**

A more formal statement of the same point is the invariance of the spacetime interval, $c^{2}\Delta t^{2}-\Delta x^{2}$. Evaluated in the Earth frame with the exact journey time $t=\sqrt{73}\ \mathrm{yr}$, it is $73-8.0^{2}=9$ (in $\mathrm{ly^{2}}$); in the spacecraft frame the two events occur at the same place, so it is $3.0^{2}-0=9$. The frames disagree about $\Delta t$ and $\Delta x$ separately but agree on the interval, which is the proper time, $3.0$ yr.  **(R1)**
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The proper-time identification is essential — award (M1) only if $\tau=t/\gamma$ is used (i.e. the spacecraft time is the *shorter* one). Candidates who write $t=\gamma\tau$ with $t=8.0/\beta$ inverted forfeit the method. Accept $\gamma=2.85$ and $v=0.936c$; allow $0.94c$ at 2 s.f.

(b) Watch for the direction of the contraction: the proper length is the Earth-frame length, so the spacecraft length is *smaller*. Award at most one mark for $L=\gamma L_{0}=22.8$ ly.

(c) A common omission is the light-travel time of the message. Award the first two marks even if the candidate then forgets to add them.

(d) The mark scheme is looking for two ideas: the contracted distance from (b), and the fact that the relative speed is below $c$ in both frames. 'Time passes more slowly for the astronauts' on its own is not an explanation of the distance and earns nothing.

(a) Alternative method: eliminate $\gamma$ first by writing $t=\gamma\tau$ with $t=8.0/\beta$, then solve the resulting equation in $\beta$; award full marks provided the proper time is identified. Accept $\gamma$ in the range 2.83–2.87 and $\beta$ in 0.93–0.94. Carry at least three significant figures through the working; a final answer rounded to 2 s.f. ($0.94c$) is acceptable.
questions.explanation:
The awkward step is part (a): the speed is the unknown, and it appears *inside* $\gamma$, so the equation $3.0=\frac{8.0}{\beta}\sqrt{1-\beta^{2}}$ has to be solved algebraically before any number appears. Students who are used to being handed $v$ and asked for $\gamma$ often freeze here, or try to guess-and-check with a calculator.

The second idea is that there are two different 'distances' and two different 'times' in the problem, and the question only makes sense once you know which is the proper one:

- The Earth–star separation is a proper **length** (endpoints at rest in the Earth frame) → it is the largest value, $8.0$ ly.
- The journey duration is a proper **time** (both events at the same place in the spacecraft) → it is the smallest value, $3.0$ yr.

Mixing these up is the single most common error, and it is self-consistent enough to look right: it gives $\gamma=1/2.85$ and $v$ still below $c$, so nothing 'feels' wrong.

Part (c) is a separate trap — the message takes 8 years to get home, nearly as long as the journey took in the Earth frame, and omitting it is the standard slip.

The payoff in (d) is the resolution: the astronauts are not 'travelling faster than light'; they simply have less distance to cover. Both observers agree on the relative speed and on the physical outcome; they disagree about how much distance and how much time were involved.

A third wrong turn looks like a paradox: dividing the Earth-frame distance $8.0$ ly by the spacecraft-frame time $3.0$ yr gives a quotient greater than $c$, which is then read as superluminal travel. The error is mixing frames — speed is a distance divided by a time *within a single frame*, and these two quantities belong to different frames. Computed consistently, the Earth observer divides $8.0$ ly by $8.54$ yr and the astronauts divide $2.81$ ly by $3.0$ yr, and both quotients give $0.936c$. A result above $c$ is a signal that the numerator and the denominator were taken from different reference frames.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the A.5 bullets on time dilation and length contraction. The problem was constructed backwards: $\beta=8/\sqrt{73}$ and $\gamma=\sqrt{73}/3$ were chosen so that the algebra yields exact surds, giving $v=0.936c$ and a contracted distance of $2.81$ ly that reproduces the stated 3.0 yr exactly.

verification.method: gamma and beta recomputed; cross-checked with gamma = sqrt(73)/3 = 2.848, L = 8/gamma = 2.81 ly, 2.81/0.936 = 3.0 yr

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: B.3 Gas laws (ideal gas equation), B.4 Thermodynamics (AHL): first law, work, internal energy, heat engine efficiency
questions.topic: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
questions.challenge_mechanism: The cycle looks like a simple rectangle but requires three separate ideas to be combined: temperature ratios from the gas laws, work as area, and the first law applied to only the two legs where heat flows in — and then the efficiency has to be read against a Carnot bound the student must supply themselves.
questions.stimulus:
A fixed amount of monatomic ideal gas is taken round the rectangular cycle ABCDA shown in the table. Each leg is either isochoric (constant volume) or isobaric (constant pressure).

| State | $p$ / Pa | $V$ / m³ | $T$ / K |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | $2.0\times10^{5}$ | $5.0\times10^{-3}$ | $300$ |
| B | $4.0\times10^{5}$ | $5.0\times10^{-3}$ |  |
| C | $4.0\times10^{5}$ | $1.0\times10^{-2}$ |  |
| D | $2.0\times10^{5}$ | $1.0\times10^{-2}$ |  |

For a monatomic ideal gas, $U=\dfrac32 nRT$. The amount of gas is $n=0.40\ \mathrm{mol}$ and $R=8.31\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$.
questions.question: The cycle runs A → B → C → D → A.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net work done by the gas in one complete cycle.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total thermal energy transferred **to** the gas during one complete cycle.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the efficiency of this cycle as a heat engine, and compare it with the efficiency of a Carnot engine operating between the same maximum and minimum temperatures.

questions.answer:
**(a)**  From $pV=nRT$, with $n$ and $R$ constant, $T\propto pV$.

A → B is isochoric, so $T\propto p$:  $\dfrac{T_{B}}{T_{A}}=\dfrac{p_{B}}{p_{A}}=\dfrac{4.0}{2.0}=2 \Rightarrow T_{B}=600\ \mathrm{K}$.  **(M1)(A1)**

B → C is isobaric, so $T\propto V$:  $\dfrac{T_{C}}{T_{B}}=\dfrac{V_{C}}{V_{B}}=\dfrac{1.0\times10^{-2}}{5.0\times10^{-3}}=2 \Rightarrow T_{C}=1200\ \mathrm{K}$.  **(A1)**

C → D is isochoric:  $\dfrac{T_{D}}{T_{C}}=\dfrac{p_{D}}{p_{C}}=\dfrac{2.0}{4.0}=\dfrac12 \Rightarrow T_{D}=600\ \mathrm{K}$.  **(A1)**

(Consistency check: D → A is isobaric with $\frac{V_A}{V_D}=\frac12$, giving $T_{A}=300\ \mathrm{K}$ as stated.)

**(b)**  Work is done only on the two isochoric-free legs:

B → C:  $W=p\,\Delta V=4.0\times10^{5}(1.0\times10^{-2}-5.0\times10^{-3})=4.0\times10^{5}(5.0\times10^{-3})=2000\ \mathrm{J}$  **(A1)**

D → A:  $W=p\,\Delta V=2.0\times10^{5}(5.0\times10^{-3}-1.0\times10^{-2})=-1000\ \mathrm{J}$  **(A1)**

$$W_{\text{net}}=2000-1000=1000\ \mathrm{J}$$  **(A1)**

(Equivalently, the area of the rectangle: $(4.0-2.0)\times10^{5}\times(1.0-0.5)\times10^{-2}=1000\ \mathrm{J}$.)

**(c)**  Heat flows **in** during the two legs where the temperature rises: A → B and B → C.

**A → B (isochoric):**  $W=0$, so by the first law $Q=\Delta U$.

$$Q_{AB}=\tfrac32 nR\,\Delta T=\tfrac32(0.40)(8.31)(600-300)=1.5(0.40)(8.31)(300)=1496\ \mathrm{J}$$  **(M1)(A1)**

**B → C (isobaric):**  $\Delta U=\tfrac32 nR\,\Delta T=\tfrac32(0.40)(8.31)(1200-600)=2992\ \mathrm{J}$  **(A1)**

$W=2000\ \mathrm{J}$ from (b), so by the first law $Q=\Delta U+W$:

$$Q_{BC}=2992+2000=4992\ \mathrm{J}$$  **(M1)(A1)**

$$Q_{\text{in}}=1496+4992=6488\approx6.5\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{J}$$

**(d)**

$$\eta=\frac{W_{\text{net}}}{Q_{\text{in}}}=\frac{1000}{6488}=0.154=15.4\%$$  **(A1)**

A Carnot engine between $T_{\max}=1200\ \mathrm{K}$ and $T_{\min}=300\ \mathrm{K}$ has

$$\eta_{\text{Carnot}}=1-\frac{T_{\min}}{T_{\max}}=1-\frac{300}{1200}=0.75=75\%$$  **(M1)(A1)**

So this cycle achieves only about one fifth of the Carnot efficiency.  **(A1)**  The reason is that heat is taken in over a whole *range* of temperatures — including during the isochoric leg A → B, where the gas is still relatively cool — and rejected over a range as well (C → D and D → A). A Carnot engine takes in all of its heat at the single highest temperature and rejects it all at the single lowest; any engine that absorbs heat while its temperature is changing must do worse.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) Credit either the ratio argument or direct substitution into $T=pV/nR$. Using $R=8.31$ and $n=0.40$ gives $T_{A}=301\ \mathrm{K}$ rather than exactly $300\ \mathrm{K}$; this is rounding in the data and must not be penalised. Award full marks for temperatures given as 600, 1200, 600 K.

(b) Award (A1) for each leg's work with the correct sign, (A1) for the net. Credit the 'area of the p–V loop' method fully if the area is correctly identified as $(p_{2}-p_{1})(V_{2}-V_{1})$.

(c) The key discrimination is *which* legs to include. Candidates who sum $\Delta U$ over the whole cycle get zero (correctly, since it returns to A) and conclude $Q_{\text{in}}=W_{\text{net}}$, which is wrong — heat is also *rejected*. Award (M1) for applying $Q=\Delta U+W$ on a heating leg. Condone 6.4–6.5 kJ given rounding.

(d) Accept 15%–16%. The Carnot comparison must use the *extreme* temperatures of the cycle (300 K and 1200 K), not the mean. The final (A1) is for an explanation in terms of heat being absorbed/rejected across a temperature range; 'real engines are always less efficient' is not sufficient.
questions.explanation:
This question is assembled from three ideas students usually meet separately, and the joins are where the marks are lost.

First, the temperatures. No absolute calculation is needed if you notice that each leg holds either $p$ or $V$ fixed, so $T\propto pV$ collapses to a simple ratio. Candidates who insist on computing $T=pV/nR$ for every state do more work and accumulate rounding error (the data are only self-consistent to about 0.3%).

Second, and this is the real trap: **the net work is not the net heat**. Over a complete cycle $\Delta U=0$, so $W_{\text{net}}=Q_{\text{in}}-Q_{\text{out}}$ — but 'the total heat transferred to the gas' means $Q_{\text{in}}$ only, i.e. the two legs on which the temperature rises. A very common answer to (c) is $1000\ \mathrm{J}$, arrived at by applying $\Delta U=0$ to the whole cycle and forgetting the rejected heat entirely. The efficiency then comes out as 100%, which should be an immediate alarm bell.

Third, the Carnot comparison. Students often reach for the temperatures of the *isothermal* legs — but there are none here. The correct bound uses the extreme temperatures the working substance actually reaches, 300 K and 1200 K, giving 75%. The gap between 15% and 75% is then the physical point: a cycle that absorbs heat while warming up is inherently wasteful, which is why real engines use regeneration and why the Carnot ideal insists on isothermal heat exchange.

Classic wrong turns: including C → D in $Q_{\text{in}}$; using $W=p\Delta V$ on the isochoric legs; and quoting the Carnot efficiency with temperatures in the wrong order (giving a negative value).

provenance.adaptation: Built from the B.3 (ideal gas) and B.4 (first law, efficiency) bullets. The rectangular cycle was chosen so that every leg is either isochoric or isobaric (no isothermal leg, hence no shortcut), and the numbers were picked so the net work is exactly 1000 J and the Carnot bound is a clean 75%.

verification.method: each leg recomputed via Q = dU + W; energy balance checked: Q_in - Q_out = 1000 J (Q_out = 5488 J over C->D and D->A)

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: C.5 Doppler effect (AHL): moving source, moving observer, reflection
questions.challenge_mechanism: The Doppler shift has to be applied twice — once for the outgoing trip and once for the reflection — and the two shifts compose multiplicatively, not additively. The final part asks for a small-speed approximation to be derived, which most students can only do by guessing.
questions.question: A bat flies in a straight line at $6.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ towards a vertical wall, emitting ultrasound of frequency $40.0\ \mathrm{kHz}$. The speed of sound in still air is $340\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Assume the air is still and the bat flies perpendicular to the wall.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of the ultrasound that arrives at the wall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The ultrasound reflects from the wall. Calculate the frequency of the reflected sound received back at the bat.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that the received frequency is given by $f''=f\dfrac{v+u}{v-u}$, where $u$ is the speed of the bat and $v$ the speed of sound.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the exact difference between the emitted and received frequencies. Show further that when $u\ll v$ this difference is approximately $\dfrac{2fu}{v}$, and comment on the accuracy of the approximation here.

questions.answer:
**(a)**  The source (bat) moves towards a stationary observer (the wall):

$$f'=f\frac{v}{v-u}=40.0\times10^{3}\times\frac{340}{340-6.0}$$  **(M1)(A1)**

$$=40.0\times10^{3}\times\frac{340}{334}=40.0\times10^{3}(1.01796)=40.7\ \mathrm{kHz}$$  **(A1)**

(more precisely $40\,719\ \mathrm{Hz}$)

As a check, the shift is small and positive: $u/v=0.0176$, so a $1.8\%$ increase in frequency is physically reasonable.  **(R1)**

**(b)**  The wall reflects the sound; it behaves as a **stationary source** emitting frequency $f'$. The bat is now a moving **observer** approaching that source:

$$f''=f'\frac{v+u}{v}=40\,719\times\frac{340+6.0}{340}=40\,719\times1.01765$$  **(M1)(A1)**

$$=41\,437\ \mathrm{Hz}=41.4\ \mathrm{kHz}$$  **(A1)(A1)**

Cross-check: the two successive factors multiply, $1.01796\times1.01765=1.03593$, which equals $346/334$ directly, confirming that the shifts compose multiplicatively.  **(R1)**

**(c)**  Combining the two shifts:

$$f''=\left(f\frac{v}{v-u}\right)\left(\frac{v+u}{v}\right)=f\frac{v+u}{v-u}$$  **(M1)(A1)(A1)(A1)**

— the $v$ factors cancel, which is why the two shifts **multiply** rather than add.

**(d)**  Exact difference:  $f''-f=41\,437-40\,000=1437\ \mathrm{Hz}\approx1.44\ \mathrm{kHz}$.  **(A1)**

For $u\ll v$:

$$\frac{v+u}{v-u}=\frac{1+u/v}{1-u/v}=\left(1+\frac{u}{v}\right)\left(1-\frac{u}{v}\right)^{-1}\approx\left(1+\frac{u}{v}\right)\left(1+\frac{u}{v}\right)$$  **(M1)**

using the binomial expansion $(1-x)^{-1}\approx1+x$ for small $x$. Hence

$$f''\approx f\left(1+\frac{u}{v}\right)^{2}\approx f\left(1+\frac{2u}{v}\right),$$

neglecting the $(u/v)^{2}$ term, so

$$f''-f\approx\frac{2fu}{v}.$$  **(A1)**

Numerically:  $\dfrac{2fu}{v}=\dfrac{2(40\,000)(6.0)}{340}=1412\ \mathrm{Hz}$.  **(A1)**

Compared with the exact $1437\ \mathrm{Hz}$, the approximation is low by about $1.7\%$ — reasonable, since $u/v=0.0176$ and the neglected term is of order $(u/v)^{2}\approx3\times10^{-4}$ relative to the leading correction, i.e. roughly $1.8\%$ of the shift. The approximation is excellent for $u/v<0.01$.

The approximation is the first two terms of the expansion $\left(1+\frac{u}{v}\right)^{2}=1+\frac{2u}{v}+\left(\frac{u}{v}\right)^{2}+\dots$, so the leading neglected term is $(u/v)^{2}$ relative to unity — about $1.8\%$ of the $2u/v$ shift, as quoted. In the limit $u\to v$ the exact ratio $(v+u)/(v-u)$ diverges while the linear form $1+2u/v$ stays finite, which shows the approximation must not be used at high speed.  **(R1)**
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) Award (M1) for selecting the moving-source formula $f'=fv/(v-u)$. Candidates who use the moving-observer formula here forfeit the method mark. Accept 40.7 kHz.

(b) The crucial idea is that the reflection makes the wall a *source* of frequency $f'$ (not $f$). Award (M1) for that step, (A1) for the moving-observer formula, (A1) for substitution, (A1) for 41.4 kHz. Candidates who apply the shift a second time to $f$ instead of $f'$ get $43.4$ kHz and forfeit everything after the first mark.

(c) Award full marks for the cancellation argument. A candidate who writes 'the shifts add: $f''=f(1+2u/v)$' as an identity has not shown the exact result and earns at most one mark.

(d) Accept 1437–1440 Hz for the exact value and 1410–1415 Hz for the approximation. The comment must be quantitative (a percentage or a comparison of the two numbers); 'it is quite accurate' alone is not creditworthy.

(b) Alternative method: quote the combined result $f''=f(v+u)/(v-u)$ from (c) and substitute directly; award full marks even if the two stages are not shown separately. Follow through from (a): a candidate with an incorrect $f'$ who nevertheless applies the correct moving-observer factor keeps the later marks. Accept 41.3–41.5 kHz, and allow three or four significant figures throughout.
questions.explanation:
The single idea that separates correct from incorrect here is that a reflection applies the Doppler shift **twice**: once because the source is moving relative to the wall, and once again because the bat is moving relative to the sound coming back. The two shifts compose multiplicatively, and the speed of sound cancels out of the product — which is why the clean result is $f''=f\frac{v+u}{v-u}$ and not something involving $v^{2}$.

Students typically make one of two errors. Either they apply the shift only once (getting 40.7 kHz, which is the answer to part (a) and not to part (b)), or they apply the *same* formula twice to the original frequency $f$, getting $f(v/(v-u))^{2}=43.4$ kHz — a plausible-looking number that is wrong because the wall is not a moving source.

Part (d) then asks for something rarely practised: deriving the small-speed approximation rather than being handed it. The trick is to write the ratio as $\frac{1+u/v}{1-u/v}$ and expand the denominator binomially. Doing it the other way round — expanding $f(v+u)/(v-u)$ directly — is messier and most students who try it lose the factor of 2.

The physical context matters too: this is exactly how bat echolocation and police speed radar work. The measured quantity is not the absolute frequency but the *beat* between emitted and received signals, and for $u\ll v$ that beat is $2fu/v$ — linear in the target speed, which is what makes it a useful speed measurement.

Classic wrong turns: adding $u$ instead of subtracting it in the denominator; using $v-u$ for the approaching observer in (b); and forgetting that $u/v$ must be dimensionless (all speeds in the same units).

provenance.adaptation: Built from the C.5 bullets on the Doppler effect for moving source and moving observer. The reflection scenario and the requirement to derive the $2fu/v$ approximation via binomial expansion are the original elements; the numbers ($u=6.0$, $v=340$) were chosen so the approximation is accurate to about 2%, making the final comment meaningful rather than trivially exact.

verification.method: both stages recomputed independently; exact 41437 Hz cross-checked against f(346/334) = 40000 x 1.035928 = 41437 Hz

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: E.3 Radioactive decay (AHL): decay constant, activity, half-life, exponential decay
questions.topic: Theme E: Nuclear and quantum physics
questions.challenge_mechanism: A two-component decay: two isotopes with half-lives differing by a factor of eight are mixed, and their separate initial activities have to be recovered from only the total activity at two times — which means solving simultaneous equations in exponentials, then solving a logarithmic equation for the crossover time.
questions.question:
A sample contains a mixture of two radioactive isotopes, P and Q. Isotope P has a half-life of $4.0\ \mathrm{h}$ and isotope Q has a half-life of $32\ \mathrm{h}$.

At time $t=0$ the **total** activity of the sample is $1200\ \mathrm{kBq}$. At $t=16\ \mathrm{h}$ the total activity is $300\ \mathrm{kBq}$.

Assume that the decay products are stable and that the two isotopes decay independently.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down an expression for the activity of each isotope at time $t$, in terms of its initial activity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the initial activity of each isotope, showing the pair of simultaneous equations you solve. Give both values in $\mathrm{kBq}$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the activity of each isotope at $t=16\ \mathrm{h}$ and hence verify that the total is $300\ \mathrm{kBq}$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the time at which the two isotopes contribute equally to the total activity.

questions.answer:
**(a)**  Using $A=A_{0}2^{-t/T_{1/2}}$:

$$A_{P}(t)=A_{P0}\,2^{-t/4.0},\qquad A_{Q}(t)=A_{Q0}\,2^{-t/32}$$  **(A1)(A1)**

(with $t$ in hours)

Equivalently $A(t)=A_{0}e^{-\lambda t}$ with $\lambda=\ln2/T_{1/2}$; the two forms are identical because $2^{-t/T_{1/2}}=e^{-(\ln2)t/T_{1/2}}$. For P, $\lambda_{P}=\ln2/4.0=0.173\ \mathrm{h^{-1}}$; for Q, $\lambda_{Q}=\ln2/32=0.0217\ \mathrm{h^{-1}}$.  **(R1)**

**(b)**  Let $A_{P0}=a$ and $A_{Q0}=b$.

At $t=0$:  $a+b=1200$  **(A1)**

At $t=16\ \mathrm{h}$: P has undergone $\dfrac{16}{4}=4$ half-lives and Q has undergone $\dfrac{16}{32}=0.5$ half-lives:

$$a\,2^{-4}+b\,2^{-0.5}=300$$  **(M1)(A1)**

$$\frac{a}{16}+0.7071\,b=300$$

Substituting $b=1200-a$:

$$0.0625a+0.7071(1200-a)=300$$  **(M1)**

$$0.0625a+848.5-0.7071a=300 \Rightarrow -0.6446a=-548.5$$

$$a=851\ \mathrm{kBq},\qquad b=1200-851=349\ \mathrm{kBq}$$  **(A1)(A1)**

Because the decay factors are known numbers, these two equations are linear in $a$ and $b$, which is why two total-activity readings suffice to recover both initial activities. If the two half-lives were equal the equations would be linearly dependent and no unique solution would exist; the eightfold separation of the half-lives is what makes the recovery possible.  **(R1)**

**(c)**  At $t=16\ \mathrm{h}$:

$$A_{P}=851\times2^{-4}=\frac{851}{16}=53.2\ \mathrm{kBq}$$  **(A1)**

$$A_{Q}=349\times2^{-0.5}=\frac{349}{1.414}=246.8\ \mathrm{kBq}$$  **(A1)**

$$\text{Total}=53.2+246.8=300\ \mathrm{kBq}\ \checkmark$$  **(A1)**

**(d)**  Set the two contributions equal:

$$a\,2^{-t/4}=b\,2^{-t/32}$$  **(M1)**

$$\frac{a}{b}=2^{\,t/4-t/32}=2^{\,7t/32}$$  **(A1)**

$$\frac{851}{349}=2.438=2^{\,7t/32}$$

$$\frac{7t}{32}=\log_{2}(2.438)=\frac{\ln 2.438}{\ln 2}=\frac{0.8913}{0.6931}=1.286$$  **(M1)**

$$t=\frac{32}{7}(1.286)=5.88\ \mathrm{h}\approx5.9\ \mathrm{h}$$  **(A1)**

Check:  $A_{P}=851\times2^{-5.88/4}=851\times0.361=307\ \mathrm{kBq}$ and $A_{Q}=349\times2^{-5.88/32}=349\times0.880=307\ \mathrm{kBq}$ ✓

As a limiting check, the crossover must fall after both isotopes are still appreciable and before the fast isotope dominates: $t=5.9\ \mathrm{h}$ lies between $T_{1/2,P}=4.0\ \mathrm{h}$ and $T_{1/2,Q}=32\ \mathrm{h}$, as required. Physically this is the time at which the sample stops behaving like P and starts behaving like Q.  **(R1)**
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) Accept the equivalent exponential forms $A=A_{0}e^{-\lambda t}$ with $\lambda_{P}=\ln2/4.0=0.173\ \mathrm{h^{-1}}$ and $\lambda_{Q}=\ln2/32=0.0217\ \mathrm{h^{-1}}$.

(b) Award (M1) for recognising 4 and 0.5 half-lives respectively — a candidate who uses 16/32 = 0.5 correctly but writes $2^{-16/32}$ as $2^{-2}$ has mis-handled the exponent. Follow through on small rounding differences; accept $a$ in the range 845–855 kBq and $b$ in 345–355 kBq. The pair must sum to 1200.

(c) Follow through on the candidate's values from (b); the verification is the point of this part, so a total that does not come to 300 kBq signals an error in (b) and should not be credited here either.

(d) The discriminating step is combining the exponents: $2^{-t/4}/2^{-t/32}=2^{-7t/32}$. Candidates who write $2^{-t/4-t/32}$ (adding instead of subtracting) will get a negative time. Award (M1) for equating the two expressions, (A1) for the correct exponent arithmetic, (M1) for taking logs, (A1) for 5.9 h. Allow 5.8–6.0 h.
questions.explanation:
Single-isotope decay questions are routine; this one is not, because there are two unknowns and only one decay curve's worth of data — the *total* activity at two times. That forces a simultaneous solution, and the exponential terms cannot be combined, so there is no shortcut.

The two places where work collapses:

1. **Part (b) is really a pair of simultaneous equations.** Recognising that 16 h is 4 half-lives for P but only half a half-life for Q is straightforward; the difficulty is then carrying $2^{-0.5}=0.7071$ through the algebra without rounding it to 0.7 (which shifts the answer by about 20 kBq).
2. **Part (d) needs the exponent law applied to a difference.** $\dfrac{2^{-t/4}}{2^{-t/32}}=2^{-t/4+t/32}=2^{-7t/32}$ — most candidates either add the exponents or subtract them the wrong way round and obtain a negative time, which they then either report or 'fix' by changing a sign without understanding why.

Worth noticing afterwards: the fast isotope P starts with the larger activity (851 vs 349 kBq) but by 16 h it contributes almost nothing (53 kBq against 247 kBq). That is what the crossover time of 5.9 h means physically — the mixture's behaviour is dominated by P early on and by Q later, and any measurement of 'the' half-life of the sample would give a value that drifts continuously from near 4 h towards 32 h. That is why mixed sources are awkward in practice, and why a single half-life measurement on an unknown sample is not enough to identify it.

Classic wrong turns: treating the sample as having a single effective half-life; using $A=A_{0}e^{-\lambda t}$ with $\lambda$ in hours but $t$ in seconds; and rounding $2^{-0.5}$ prematurely.
